title: Sugar
subtitle: 1970–today · Corn Syrup, Obesity and the Sugar Tax: From Yudkin’s Warning to the Soft Drinks Levy

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Cyclamates and saccharin, the Farm Bill, the end of the US quota, the WTO, the WHO guideline and the sugar taxes of Mexico and Britain

entries.label: Egypt’s republic subsidises sugar with bread and fuel
entries.hint: Consumer subsidies — above all cheap baladi bread, but also cooking oil, sugar and fuel — have been the Egyptian republic’s basic social contract since Nasser; every attempt to cut them (1977, 2013, 2017, 2024) has been politically fraught, and from 2014 a smart-card ration system targets the support. Sugar here is a staple of a state’s promise to its citizens, not a tax base as in Iran or Britain.
entries.note: SECONDARY (via this atlas): egypt-1952-today::e8 (and c6 on the bread riots of 1977); that entry’s own sources were not re-checked here. Compare sugar-1900-1970::o11 and the British rationing of o8 in that folio.

entries.label: The FDA bans cyclamates
entries.hint: Calcium cyclamate, used in diet drinks from 1952, is banned by the FDA in 1970 after laboratory studies of the late 1960s suggest it may cause cancer. By the late 1970s most diet products are made with a third sugar substitute, aspartame (NutraSweet, Equal).
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith, Sugar: A Global History (2015) p.129; Walvin, Sugar: The World Corrupted (2017) ch.15 (concern over artificial sweeteners in the 1960s and ’70s and FDA scrutiny). See te2.

entries.label: The 1973 Farm Bill lets corn farmers grow as much as they like
entries.hint: The 1973 Farm Bill devises a payment letting farmers grow as much corn as they want while guaranteeing a profit through federal subsidies; the high-fructose corn syrup first made in 1957 then becomes cheap. Walvin calls American obesity ‘itself subsidised by American taxes’: $5.7 billion went to corn in 1983 alone.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15 (the Bill, the 1983 subsidy and the characterisation are his).

entries.label: Congress ends the US sugar quota system
entries.hint: In 1974 Congress ends the old quota system, the Sugar Act of 1937, that had protected US sugar interests and controlled prices; the drinks and confectionery lobbies hoped for cheaper sugar, but prices first jumped and then fluctuated wildly. By the late 1970s the US sugar industry wanted federal protection back, and the soft-drink makers, tired of volatile world prices, began to look for another sweetener.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15 (‘in 1974 the old sugar quota system … was ended by Congress’) and ch.11 (the Act of 1937 ‘remained in place until 1974’). See sugar-1900-1970::o7 and te1.

entries.label: Saccharin is put under a moratorium, then cleared
entries.hint: In 1977 a Canadian study reports that saccharin caused cancer in test animals and the FDA places a moratorium on its use until more studies are done; later studies did not confirm the result and the ban is lifted in 1991.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.129 (‘the ban was lifted in 1991’; the wording ‘placed a moratorium’ is Smith’s).

entries.label: The WTO is launched to end farm subsidies, but rich countries keep theirs
entries.hint: The World Trade Organisation, launched in 1995, was meant to end farm subsidies and trade restrictions, but poor countries were pressed by the World Bank and IMF to open their markets while rich ones kept their subsidies; the largest recipients of European subsidies in 2009 were the big transnational sugar companies, and the Wall Street Journal in 2015 called the US federal sugar program’s absurdity ‘legendary’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14 (the claim about the WTO’s record is his argument). The WTO’s 2004–05 rulings against the EU’s sugar export subsidies (a case brought by Brazil, Australia and Thailand) are general knowledge and were not found in the sources read.

entries.label: The House votes a Personal Responsibility in Food Consumption Act
entries.hint: In 2004–05 the US House of Representatives approves a bill with the title The Personal Responsibility in Food Consumption Act, reflecting the food and drink industry’s fear of the fate of tobacco, hit in 2004 by threats of astronomical damages ($280 billion) for health damage. Walvin says that by 2004 obesity, and the role of sugar in it, was being widely compared to tobacco in the United States.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13 (the bill is not described beyond its title there).

entries.label: Mexico taxes sugary drinks
entries.hint: Mexico’s 10 per cent tax on sugar-sweetened drinks, introduced in January 2014, is followed by a fall in purchases of taxed drinks of about 6 per cent in the first year (12 per cent by December) and 9.7 per cent in 2015, largest among the poorest households; Walvin’s account is of ‘a fall of 6–9 per cent in soft-drink sales, most striking among the poor’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.16 (no year given); web summaries of the Colchero team’s studies, BMJ (2016) and Health Affairs (2017) — observational before-and-after comparisons, which show association, not proof of cause. The tax is one peso a litre in those reports.

entries.label: The WHO recommends free sugars below 10 per cent of energy
entries.hint: In March 2015 the World Health Organization recommends, as a ‘strong’ recommendation, that adults and children reduce their intake of free sugars to less than 10 per cent of total energy, and suggests, ‘conditionally’, below 5 per cent — about 25 grams, six teaspoons a day. It rests on evidence about body weight and dental caries, which the WHO rates low to moderate quality.
entries.note: SECONDARY (web summaries of the WHO news release and guideline; the full text was not read). The US American Heart Association had set limits of five teaspoons for women and nine for men in 2009 (t5).

entries.label: Britain announces a soft-drinks levy
entries.hint: After Public Health England’s Sugar Reduction report blamed sugar in October 2015 and The Times and others urged a tax, the British Cabinet is won over, and the 2016 Budget announces a Soft Drinks Industry Levy from April 2018 — 18p a litre for drinks with over 5 g of sugar per 100 ml, 24p over 8 g. Makers reformulate so quickly that the forecast revenue for the first year falls from £520 million to £240 million.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.16 (the 2015 report, the press campaign, ‘agreed to introduce a tax on sugary drinks in 2018’); web summaries (Birketts, FoodNavigator, LSE, Cambridge MRC Epidemiology Unit) for the rates, the date of 6 April 2018 and the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts.

entries.label: The EU’s sugar quotas end
entries.hint: The European Union’s sugar production quotas, a regime that had held in violation of its WTO export commitments, end on 30 September 2017 under the 2013 reform of the Common Agricultural Policy; a study of 2018 finds a significant impact on prices from the market surplus.
entries.note: SECONDARY (web summaries: Commission announcements, a USDA report and an IDEAS-indexed 2018 paper; none read in full). Compare Smith (2015) p.50 (Europe a net exporter of sugar by the end of the twentieth century).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Energy drinks, supersizing, advertising to children and ‘Zero Sugar’

entries.label: McDonald’s ‘large’ and ‘supersize’
entries.hint: In the 1950s McDonald’s sold one size of fries; in 1972 it offers ‘large size’ and in 1994 ‘supersized fries’, promoted with the phrase ‘Supersize It!’; with cheap corn sweetener, Coca-Cola likewise goes from 12 oz to 20 oz and 64 oz ‘buckets’ — ‘it paid to go big’. By 2000 McDonald’s is Coca-Cola’s biggest customer.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15 (the fries passage).

entries.label: Lucozade and Red Bull sell sugar as energy
entries.hint: A British pharmaceutical firm picked up the Lucozade formula and, in 1983, repositioned it from a convalescent drink as an energy drink (‘Lucozade replaces lost energy’); Red Bull — caffeine, sucrose, glucose and other ingredients — is launched in Europe in 1987. The first sports drink, Gatorade, was formulated in 1965 at the University of Florida.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) pp.122–123 (PDF 124).

entries.label: Three-quarters of advertisements aimed at children are for foods of ‘low nutritional quality’
entries.hint: A 2013 study of 577 food advertisements aimed at children finds that nearly three-quarters promoted foods of ‘low nutritional quality’; in 2001–02 Coca-Cola spent £23 million, Walkers Crisps £16.5 million and Müller’s pot desserts £13 million on advertising in Britain. Walvin counts marketing as the means by which sugar reached its present levels.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13 (the study unnamed) and ch.16.

entries.label: Jamie Oliver calls sugar ‘the next tobacco’
entries.hint: The celebrity chef Jamie Oliver, with a huge television following, calls sugar ‘the next tobacco’ in the campaign of 2015 that followed the Public Health England report; medical authorities had already been making the same comparison, and critics of fast food in public places answered those who called such ideas intrusive by pointing to the fight over smoking.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.16.

entries.label: Coca-Cola advertises ‘Zero Sugar’
entries.hint: In the summer of 2016 millions of British television viewers are bombarded by advertisements proclaiming Coca-Cola to be ‘Zero Sugar’: Walvin says the game was up for sugar and the company was forced to put much of its corporate might behind the ‘zero’ idea. The firm had launched its own bottled water in 1999.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.16 and conclusion (his interpretation).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Yudkin, Sugar Blues, the bliss point, the AHA limits, the Lancet, PHE and the 2016 exposure of the industry’s research

entries.label: Yudkin’s Pure, White and Deadly
entries.hint: John Yudkin, who built Queen Elizabeth College’s nutrition department and was Professor of Nutrition at London from 1954 to 1971, publishes Pure, White and Deadly in 1972 (Sweet and Dangerous in the USA); it argues that sugar is involved in tooth decay, overweight, diabetes and heart disease. Smith calls it ‘a tirade’ that stirred the public but was rejected by the medical community, which held dietary fat to be the cause of heart disease.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.131; Yudkin, Pure, White and Deadly (1986 edition) front matter and p.vii (publication history, expanded in 1986 with a chapter ‘Attack is the best defence’ on the sugar industry’s reaction). Yudkin is an interested party; the later fate of his case is discussed in Walvin (2017) ch.14 (‘the denigration and belittling of serious researchers’).

entries.label: Duffy’s Sugar Blues
entries.hint: William Duffy, an American journalist and macrobiotic advocate, publishes the best-selling Sugar Blues in 1975 on ‘the multiple physical and mental miseries caused by human consumption of refined sucrose’; Smith lists it with earlier books such as Body, Mind, and Sugar (1951) and Diabetes, Coronary Thrombosis and the Saccharine Diseases (1966).
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) pp.131–132 (the title, date and quotation as Smith gives them).

entries.label: Taste scientists look for the ‘bliss point’
entries.hint: In 1981 the sensory scientist Howard Moskowitz leaves the Army laboratories and opens a consultancy at White Plains; General Foods spends $113 million on research in 1985, looking for products that hit the ‘bliss point’, the optimum concentration of an ingredient at which sensory pleasure is greatest. Walvin presents the research as a way of making sweetness a lure for children as well as adults.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.123 (PDF 125; Moskowitz 1981); Walvin (2017) ch.14 (the ‘bliss point’ quotation). The causal reading is Walvin’s.

entries.label: ‘Liquid Candy’ names soda as a health problem
entries.hint: The Center for Science in the Public Interest publishes Liquid Candy in 2005, a report on the health effects of soft drinks; in the same year the Royal College of Surgeons’ dental division says it is seriously concerned about the state of children’s oral health in England.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.120 (PDF 122; only the title and date of the report are in the page read); Walvin (2017) ch.13 (the Royal College’s 2005 statement). See l2.

entries.label: The American Heart Association sets sugar limits
entries.hint: The American Heart Association, alarmed at a worldwide pandemic of obesity and cardiovascular disease, issues a recommended limit in 2009: five teaspoons a day of added sugar for sedentary women and nine for men, against the 22 teaspoons the average American actually ate.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13 (the numbers are his).

entries.label: The Lancet: obesity has almost doubled since 1980
entries.hint: Studies in The Lancet in 2011 report that the global prevalence of obesity has almost doubled since 1980, from 4.8 per cent of men and 7.9 per cent of women to 9.8 per cent and 13.8 per cent in 2008; some 1.3 billion people are overweight, half of them obese. The causes are many, and the research is ‘coalescing’, as a Credit Suisse report said in 2013, around sugar though medical research ‘is yet to prove conclusively’ that it is the leading cause.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.133 (PDF 135; the Credit Suisse research institute’s 2013 report is quoted by Smith).

entries.label: Public Health England’s Sugar Reduction report names sugar
entries.hint: Public Health England’s Sugar Reduction: the Evidence for Action (October 2015) says obesity and its consequences alone cost the NHS £5.1 billion a year and that the prime cause is the high concentrations of sugar in the nation’s food and drink; it gives special attention to children and to marketing, price promotions and supermarket display, and the Government, which had commissioned it, is forced to act.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.16. See o9.

entries.label: Papers reveal the sugar industry’s 1960s research strategy
entries.hint: In September 2016 papers of deceased Harvard professors show the sugar industry had paid for a review of the 1960s that played down sugar and blamed fat for heart disease; Walvin argues that for the best part of half a century sugar was ‘effectively exonerated’ and that the revelation raises the wider question of industry sponsorship of science, noting a similar story for Britain.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14; web coverage of Kearns, Schmidt and Glantz in JAMA Internal Medicine (2016). See sugar-1900-1970::t4.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Soft-drink and sweetener consumption, cereals, fast food, food-industry power, Cuba’s decline and the obesity epidemic

entries.label: American soft-drink consumption: 23 gallons in 1969, 54 in 1997
entries.hint: Per capita US consumption of soft drinks was 0.6 gallons in 1889, 3.3 in 1929, 23.4 in 1969 and 44.5 in 1985; carbonated drinks reached 54 gallons a head in 1997, with Coca-Cola controlling 45 per cent of the market (sales of $18 billion), and the per capita soft-drink total rose from 28.7 gallons in 1985 to 36.9 in 1998. The company’s sales worldwide were 1.8 billion daily servings in 2012.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15 (the figures in two places differ in definition — all drinks versus carbonated drinks — and should not be compared directly).

entries.label: Cereal sales rise from $660 million in 1970 to $4.4 billion in the 1980s
entries.hint: The sales of breakfast cereals aimed at children — ‘astonishing’ — rise from $660 million in 1970 to $4.4 billion by the mid-1980s. Since 2007, Smith says, Kellogg and General Mills, which made six of the ten unhealthiest cereals and did the most child-focused marketing, have lowered the sugar content of their children’s cereals.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14; Smith (2015) p.135 (PDF 137; the 2007 change as reported).

entries.label: America has 13,000 McDonald’s by 2001
entries.loc: The United States, Britain, Europe, India and China
entries.hint: The number of fast-food meals eaten by Americans quadruples in the twenty-five years to 1995; by 2001 the USA has more than 13,000 McDonald’s, 5,000 Burger Kings and 7,000 Pizza Huts; McDonald’s restaurants in Europe go from 1,342 in 1991 to 5,792 in 2001; by 2004 Indians and Chinese eat fast food more often than Americans. Half of Americans’ food budget goes on eating out between 1980 and 2000.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14.

entries.label: American sweetener use grows from 125 lb to 153 lb a head
entries.hint: In 1950 each American ate just over 100 lb of calorific sweeteners a year; thirty years later, over 125 lb; by 2000, 153 lb. Between 1971–74 14 per cent of Americans were obese, by the mid-1990s 22.4 per cent and by 2008 more than a third.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15. The US Department of Agriculture reckons American calorie intake rose 25 per cent between 1970 and 2010 (ch.13).

entries.label: An estimated 2 billion people are overweight in 2015
entries.hint: The World Health Organization estimates in 2015 that about 2 billion people — nearly a third of the world — are overweight and about 600 million obese, a figure doubled since 1980; childhood obesity has risen about 60 per cent since 1990, and one Briton in four is classed obese in 2013 against levels three times those of 1980. Walvin treats sugar as the main dietary cause.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13 (the attribution of cause is his argument, contested in the sources — see t6, where a 2013 research report says medical research has ‘yet to prove conclusively’ that sugar is the leading cause).

entries.label: Cuba’s sugar falls apart without the Soviet market
entries.hint: After the Soviet Union’s collapse in 1991 ends Cuba’s main market, sugar output halves from about 7 million tonnes in the early 1990s to 3.4 million in 1994–95; in 2002 the government announces the closure of nearly half of its 156 mills. By the 2020s only a score of mills run, and Al Jazeera notes that sanctions alone do not explain the decline.
entries.note: SECONDARY (web summaries only: reports from 2002 to 2023, with the mill counts varying between 155/156 and 70/71): see w2. The 1990 figure of about 8 million tonnes is as one report gives it.

entries.label: British soft-drink volumes double in twelve years
entries.hint: Walvin says the volumes of soft drinks consumed in Britain doubled between 1992 and 2004; British children are thought to consume ‘thirty times the amount of soft drinks and twenty-five times the amount of confectionery’ they did in 1950. Yudkin’s earlier figures put British soft-drink consumption at 2.7 gallons a head in 1939 and 10.7 in 1970.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13 (the ‘thirty times’ quotation is a source he cites); Yudkin (1986) p.40. The ‘doubled’ claim is Walvin’s without a table.

entries.label: Coca-Cola launches bottled water, and the market passes $150 billion
entries.hint: After ‘a great deal of hesitation’ and prompted by Pepsi, Coca-Cola launches its own bottled water in 1999, as the American consumption of tap water drops; the global bottled-water market reaches $157 billion in 2013 and is expected to reach $280 billion by 2020. In 2012 Coca-Cola’s products were sold in over 200 countries.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15.

entries.label: Nestlé’s revenue exceeds the GDP of all but seventy nations
entries.hint: Oxfam calculated in 2013 that 70 per cent of the world’s food systems were controlled by no more than 500 companies; Nestlé’s revenue in 2012 was bigger than the GDP of all but seventy of the world’s nations. Walvin contrasts wholesome foods, with profits of 3–6 per cent, with highly processed foods, with 15 per cent.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14 (Oxfam’s figure not checked).

entries.label: Hawaii has one cane grower left
entries.hint: The California and Hawaii Sugar Company dominated Hawaii’s sugar until the 1930s, when plantations began to be converted to other uses; Smith, writing in 2015, says only one cane grower remains on the islands. Its brand is now part of the American Sugar Refining Company (Domino Sugar), owned by Florida Crystals and the Sugar Cane Growers Cooperative of Florida.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) p.54. See sugar-1900-1970::ec5 for C&H.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: High-fructose corn syrup, new sweeteners, Brazil’s ethanol and the microwave

entries.label: Aspartame, sucralose and stevia reach the supermarket
entries.hint: Aspartame (NutraSweet, Equal) is in most diet products by the late 1970s; sucralose, 600 times as sweet as sugar, is approved in Canada in 1991 and the US seven years later; neotame is approved in 2002; and in 2008 the FDA approves two stevia sweeteners, Truvia (Cargill and Coca-Cola) and PureVia (PepsiCo), the following year placing purified stevia on its ‘Generally Recognized as Safe’ list. Little evidence of short-term harm has surfaced, and long-term risks, ‘if any’, remain under debate.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Smith (2015) pp.129–131; Walvin (2017) ch.15 (NutraSweet and the Monsanto conglomerate). Yudkin (1986) p.xiv argues that sweeteners are safe to use and that publicity about their risks is driven by sugar interests.

entries.label: The microwave comes to dominate the Western kitchen
entries.hint: From 1970 to 2000 the microwave oven comes to dominate the Western kitchen, alongside the supermarket’s packaged and ready-made foods — most with copious added sweeteners; Walvin links this to ‘Big Food’ and the new food system.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.14 (the sugar link is his argument).

entries.label: Brazil’s Proálcool turns cane into fuel
entries.hint: Brazil launches its Proálcool programme in 1975, answering the oil shocks of the 1970s with ethanol from sugar cane: first blended with gasoline, later pure; within about six years 90 per cent of new vehicles sold can run on ethanol. Sales fall in the 1990s as oil prices drop, and flex-fuel cars from 2003 revive it, with the building of new mills now driven by private investors rather than the state.
entries.note: SECONDARY (web summaries only: Wikipedia’s ‘History of ethanol fuel in Brazil’, the Rapid Transition site and a USP paper; none read in full; the 2003 versus 2004 date for flex-fuel cars differs between them). See w1.

entries.label: Coca-Cola switches to corn syrup
entries.hint: Coca-Cola, which had been wary of changing its main product, tries corn sweeteners in some minor drinks, finds that customers do not complain, and in 1980 switches from cane sugar to high-fructose corn syrup; in 1985 corn syrup becomes the sweetener for all its major US drinks. By the mid-1980s most soft-drink makers have switched, and HFCS is now about half of all sweeteners consumed in the USA — Yudkin records its use rising from 3 lb to 43 lb a head between 1974 and 1983.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15; Yudkin (1986) p.46 (the 1974 and 1983 figures). See o2, o3 and sugar-1900-1970::te5.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Coca-Cola’s reach and the spread of sugar taxes

entries.label: Coca-Cola is sold in over 200 countries
entries.hint: More than half of Coca-Cola’s profits are made outside the USA by 1971, although some places resisted; by 2012 it sells in over 200 countries, with 1.8 billion servings a day — one drink for every four people on the planet — and its sweetener, from the 1980s, is as often corn syrup as sugar.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.15. See sugar-1900-1970::x5.

entries.label: Sugar taxes spread from Hungary to Mexico and US cities
entries.loc: Norway, Finland, Hungary, France, Mexico and the United States
entries.hint: By 2015 various forms of sugar tax had been introduced in Norway, Finland, Hungary, France and Mexico and in some US cities, and the early evidence suggested they worked; this precedent gave the British campaign for a levy its first argument. The years of the individual taxes are not given in Walvin.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.16. The dates (for instance Hungary 2011, France 2012, Berkeley 2014) are general knowledge and not checked. See o7, o9.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The oil shocks and the Soviet collapse

entries.label: The oil shocks turn Brazil’s cane into fuel
entries.hint: The oil shocks of the 1970s lead Brazil, a large cane producer, to adopt ethanol as a fuel; sugar becomes an energy crop as well as a food, a link that the oil price still sets for cane mills.
entries.note: SECONDARY (web summaries only): see te3. The shocks’ years are conventional (1973 and 1979); the web sources say ‘1970s oil shocks’.

entries.label: The Soviet Union’s collapse ends Cuba’s sugar market
entries.hint: The Soviet Union’s collapse in 1991 removes the main buyer of Cuban sugar, which had taken the place of the American market after 1960; Soviet aid had been about 20 per cent of Cuba’s GDP in 1986–90, and the island’s economy went into a tailspin.
entries.note: SECONDARY (web summaries only). Compare sugar-1900-1970::x4 and ec7.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Overweight children, English children’s teeth and Florida’s cane workers

entries.label: Florida’s cane workers are beaten back to work
entries.hint: Importing migrant labour was a good way of circumventing local labour laws, because migrants could be moved on at the first sign of discontent; in the worst cases, in the 1980s, police were used to break up and beat up striking workers before sending them home. Investigative journalists exposed the barracks and the ecological damage, and the conditions led to a string of legal cases.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.11. See sugar-1900-1970::x3.

entries.label: Britain’s and America’s children grow heavier
entries.hint: In 2011 three in ten British boys and girls aged 2–15 are overweight or obese, and between 2011 and 2013 sixty-two children under eighteen have weight-loss surgery, against one in 2000; in the USA 32 per cent of children are overweight or obese in 2009–10 and obesity among 6–11 year olds rose from 15 to 20 per cent between 2006 and 2008.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13.

entries.label: Dental surgeons are ‘seriously concerned’ about English children’s teeth
entries.hint: In 2005 a specialist dental division of the Royal College of Surgeons says it is ‘seriously concerned about the state of children’s oral health in England’, a modern echo of what school dentists found in the first decades of the century.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Walvin (2017) ch.13. See sugar-1900-1970::l1.
